title: On Travelling: What About the People?
text:
Botanical Garden of the University of Granada. © Carolina Castillo Ferrer


Think about your last trip. Did you meet anyone from your destination? Who? In what context did that interaction take place? If you didn’t meet anyone, would you have liked to? Why? What would you have asked them? What information about the place would you have liked them to share with you? In what way do you think it would have changed your travel experience?
Leisure travel is one of the most popular recreational activities today. The latest figures from Eurostat show that 65 per cent of residents in the European Union made at least one personal leisure trip in 2024 (ec.europa.eu). People are travelling more, but are they travelling better? The answer is undoubtedly a very personal one. It will depend on what each person considers ‘better’ and on their individual preferences when it comes to travelling. In the minds of many people, however, when they think of the idea of ‘travelling’, certain notions à l’ancienne still persist: the chance to have a unique and exciting experience, to discover a different culture, to sample food with exotic flavours, to explore spectacular natural landscapes, perhaps to begin learning a language, to meet people and strike up enriching conversations with them, to acquire self-knowledge, to gain an education. The latter was the main motivation for a young Gerald Brenan to set out on his journey to the Alpujarras in 1919:

I took with me a good many books and a little money and the hope that I should be able to keep going for long enough to acquire something I badly needed — an education (South from Granada, 1957).

Nowadays, we don’t experience many of these aspects when we travel, partly due to a lack of time. We travel more frequently, but our trips are shorter and have a very tight schedule, where we feel almost obliged to tick off a list of monuments and places. But the reality is that it takes time to discover a culture, to learn a language, to get to know people, and so on. The poet Konstantin Kavafis emphasised this in the first stanza of his well-known poem “Ithaca” (1911):

When you depart for Ithaca,
wish for the road to be a long one,
full of adventure, full of knowledge.

Back when people didn’t travel as much, and those who did didn’t provide a detailed account of their journey as it unfolded on social media, it was customary, once you’d returned, to tell your close circle about your trip. Gathered together specifically to hear about it, to gain an indirect insight into that place through your experience, it was only natural that your family and friends would be interested in the sites you’d visited, the food you’d tried, whether you’d had any interesting experiences or mishaps, and, above all, the locals you’d met during your trip: ‘And what about the people?’
If you couldn’t answer that question because you hadn’t met anyone, the feeling was one of slight disappointment, as if the trip had been missing something – something very important, in fact, something intrinsic to the very concept of travel, if we once again understand travel as a source of knowledge and discovery. Having met no one, once back home, the trip made less sense, as expectations – including the natural desire to get to know or even connect with another human being from a different culture – had not been fulfilled.
Let’s be honest, almost everyone would like to meet friendly and hospitable locals when they travel, because they feel that their experience would be more enriching, more worthwhile, and probably more fun. This doesn’t always happen, and sometimes it’s quite the opposite: they have a brief interaction or run-in with an unfriendly local. That’s also part of the journey. Just ask Don Quixote!

“Well,” quoth Don Quixote, “he who reads much and walks much, sees much and knows much” (Don Quijote de la Mancha, Part Two, Chapter XXV).

Cervantes has Don Quixote articulate this aphorism that grounds learning on two pillars: reading and travelling. The Quixote, in fact, is a novel structured around the protagonist’s journeys undertaken in his quest to combat injustice in accordance with his moral codes; and on these journeys the variety and diversity of characters the Cervantine hero encounters play a central role. Before setting out on his first journey, Don Quixote’s knowledge of the world is derived from reading books, but once he is on the road, experiencing the world means interacting with other people.
Today, as always, one of the main sources of knowledge comes from social interactions. The intrepid traveller Emilia Serrano, Baroness of Wilson, stated with conviction that it was her dealings with a wide variety of people during her travels that had enabled her to confirm certain beliefs she held, such as the power of education to transform society. She expressed this in Las perlas del corazón (1875):

During my long journeys, I have witnessed events that have served as excellent lessons: I have frequented gatherings ranging from those of the highest aristocracy to the simple and modest gatherings of hard-working craftsmen, just as I have sat with genuine satisfaction in the home of a farm labourer, when, on long winter evenings, surrounded by his children and with his life partner by his side, he endeavours to inculcate, through his simple reasoning, a love of work, respect for the elderly, and courtesy towards everyone, convincing me in every social circle that education is the foundation upon which an individual becomes part of that great family known as society.

Think about your next trip — imagine travelling with the aim of having more meaningful experiences, with the time to deepen your understanding of the places you visit and connect with the people who live there. Let social interactions be a central part of our journeys so that, upon returning from our next trip and sharing our adventures and discoveries with friends and family, we can answer the question, “What about the people?”

title: About us
text:
Your placeta in Granada
La Placeta Granada was born from the idea of bringing together and connecting people from different places and backgrounds —building a great global village, respectful of both guest and host. We believe the best way to know a city is the way its own neighbours do: slowly, through daily life rather than a checklist of sights. La Placeta Granada is our invitation to step into that rhythm —real streets, real conversations, real connection.
Granada is the location we have chosen for our work, not only because of our personal ties to the city, but also because of the richness and diversity of its social and cultural ecosystem. A cradle of great artists from the medieval Al-Andalus period to the present day, its contrast of cultures – cultured, popular, religious, secular, academic, scientific, cosmopolitan and local – forms the bedrock of many of the artistic creations of artists born in, based in or passing through the city. Its past, marked by struggles and losses, by the decline and destruction of part of its historical, artistic and natural heritage, also shapes the city’s present reality.
For those of us who make up La Placeta Granada, being aware of this legacy drives us to care for it, but also to share it with those who show a genuine interest in learning about the ways of life within Granada’s culture, where – particularly in its neighbourhoods – the customs and traditions of previous generations coexist with new forms of global sociability.
Discover our programmes →

title: About us
text:
Behind every stay
Every La Placeta Granada programme is run by a small, dedicated team: specialised teaching staff and technical support committed to making each stay feel like coming home, not just visiting.
We are from Granada, we have studied at the University of Granada and have furthered our academic education abroad. Our professional experience – teaching and managing international educational programmes in Granada for over a decade – has inspired us to create La Placeta Granada, a more personal project through which we aim to develop initiatives that reflect our educational and professional philosophy, as well as our local connection, focusing on upholding the values of neighbourhood life.

title: Home

Take a seat in Granada



In Granada, a “placeta” is a hidden square where neighbours meet to share stories, time and life. Welcome to your placeta.

title: Home
text:
What is a “placeta”?
In Granada, a placeta is a small square where neighbours gather — a public space that becomes, casually and unhurriedly, a meeting point.
A few decades ago, when street life in the neighbourhoods was far more common than it is today, placetas (and their linguistic family — plazuelas, plazas, placitas) were fundamental to the fabric of community. Being in the placeta, almost daily, “made neighbourhood”: children playing freely, grandmothers keeping each other company, young people chatting for hours on a bench, and men and women who would bring down their own chairs simply to sit, talk and pass the time.

La Placeta Granada was born from that idea: bringing you into the everyday rhythm of the city, not a postcard version of it.

The user, as the data subject, is hereby informed and gives their explicit consent for their data to be incorporated into the following automated data file:

Clients and Suppliers, and for its subsequent automated processing, with La Placeta Granada being the data controller responsible for the file and its processing. The purpose of this data processing is to manage clients who request the services we provide via the Internet.

In accordance with the provisions of the GDPR, individuals have a set of fundamental rights concerning their personal data. Below, you will find detailed information on how La Placeta Granada handles each of these rights under the GDPR and in relation to your data. All our facilities and servers are located within the European Union and fully comply with the GDPR.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
1. Right to Information
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to all individuals within the European Union, the European Economic Area (EEA) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). You have the right to know what we do with your personal data, why we process it and how you may withdraw your consent at any time. This includes the right to be informed about who we are and how we handle your data.
This privacy policy applies to La Placeta Granada. The persons responsible for managing La Placeta Granada’s data are Carolina Castillo Ferrer and Patricia Molina Molina. As a general rule, you may contact them regarding any data-related concerns, as they are responsible for ensuring that your rights under the GDPR are respected.
As a business that works with both other businesses and the general public, there are several legal grounds that require us to collect and process certain personal information. The three primary legal bases under which we do this are:

To collect sufficient information to establish a service relationship.
To carry out business transactions and to retain the data necessary to process bookings and deliver the associated services.
We request your consent through various channels: by telephone, when recording your bookings, and by email, where we explicitly ask for your consent before processing any booking.

By law, we are required to retain personal data for as long as any of the three legal grounds above remain applicable. If we do not have your permission to send you emails and we have not processed any bookings from you for a period of six years, we will delete your personal data from our systems. We will also request that our third-party data processors delete this information from their systems.
If at any point you wish to withdraw your consent or lodge a complaint regarding our processing of personal data, you may do so by sending an email to info@laplacetagranada.com. We will process your withdrawal of consent or respond to your complaint within a maximum of one month from the date we receive your request.
Where clients pay by card, payment details are transmitted directly to the secure payment gateway provided by Bankinter, S.A., which stores them within its own infrastructure. La Placeta Granada does not have access to or store card details.
In line with our commitment to security and confidentiality, La Placeta Granada is particularly focused on providing our clients with the highest level of data protection. This website is served over a secure HTTPS connection, so that data transmitted between your browser and our site is encrypted.
Acceptance of the processing of your data in the manner described herein is a necessary condition for the provision of our services. The use of our services implies such acceptance, which is always revocable and without retroactive effect. The user is, in all cases, responsible for the accuracy of the data provided. La Placeta Granada reserves the right to exclude from its services any user who has provided false information, without prejudice to any other legal action that may be applicable.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
2. Right of Access
If you would like to know what personal data we hold about you, verify its accuracy and ensure that it is being processed lawfully, you may request this information by sending an email to info@laplacetagranada.com. We will provide you with all the personal data we hold about you in the same format in which your request was submitted.
We will respond within one month from the date we receive your request. If the request is particularly complex or we are dealing with a high volume of requests, we will inform you — within that initial one-month period — that we will be applying the extension permitted in such circumstances.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
3. Right to Rectification
If you believe that the information we hold about you is inaccurate or incomplete, you may inform us by sending an email to info@laplacetagranada.com. Upon receipt of your request, we will correct or update your personal data accordingly.
We will do so within one month from the date of your request. If your request is particularly complex or we are handling a high number of requests at the same time, we will notify you — within that initial one-month period — that we will be applying the extension permitted in such circumstances.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
4. Right to Erasure
Under certain circumstances, the GDPR grants you the right to request the deletion or modification of any personal data that a company may hold about you. This is also referred to as the ‘right to be forgotten’. You may request that we erase the personal information we hold about you if you believe it is no longer necessary for us to retain your data for the purposes for which it was originally collected, if you have unsubscribed or never gave consent for your data to be used for commercial purposes, or if you believe your data has been processed unlawfully. Please note that, in order to fulfil your request, we may no longer be able to provide you with our services. Alternatively, you may choose to wait until we have finished providing services to you, after which we will comply with your request in accordance with applicable law.
To submit your request, please email info@laplacetagranada.com.
We will assess your request and take the appropriate action within one month of receiving it. If the request is particularly complex or we are processing a large number of requests at the same time, we will inform you — within that one-month period — that we will apply the extension permitted in such circumstances.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
5. Right to Withdraw Consent
In accordance with the GDPR, you also have the right — under certain circumstances — to withdraw the consent you previously gave for the processing of your personal data for a specific purpose. You may request the withdrawal of your consent if you believe that the personal information we hold about you is inaccurate, if you object to the processing of your data, or if you wish us to retain the information without processing it, for example in the event that you intend to bring or defend a legal claim.
To submit your request, please email info@laplacetagranada.com.
We will evaluate and respond to your request within one month of receipt. If necessary, we will also notify any third parties involved. If your request is particularly complex or we are managing a large number of requests at the same time, we will contact you within that one-month period to let you know that additional time will be required, as permitted under the GDPR.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
6. Right to Data Portability
You have the right to request a copy of your personal data in a digital format (e.g. a spreadsheet or a text file), either for your own use or to reuse for any other lawful purpose.
To submit your request, please email info@laplacetagranada.com.
We will process your request free of charge within one month from the date of receipt. If the request is particularly complex or we are handling a large number of requests at the same time, we will inform you within that one-month period that we will make use of the extension permitted in such circumstances.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
7. Right to Object
Under certain circumstances, the GDPR grants you the right to object to the processing of your personal data, particularly if the data is inaccurate or if you do not agree with how it is being used. If you object to our processing of your personal data — whether in relation to bookings, service provision or for any other reason — you may inform us of your objection by sending an email to info@laplacetagranada.com.
If we accept your objection in writing, and while your request is being reviewed, we will stop processing your data in the manner to which you have objected. We will then restrict the processing of such data free of charge within one month, unless your request is particularly complex or we are handling a high volume of requests, in which case we will notify you within that one-month period that an extension may be required.
You will also be given the opportunity to object to receiving marketing communications from us at the time you make a booking or provide your personal data, as outlined in Section 1: Right to Information.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
section: 8. Rights Related to Automated Decision-Making and Profiling
text:
8. Rights Related to Automated Decision-Making and Profiling
We do not carry out any automated decision-making that affects your personal information.
We do not make any decisions involving what the GDPR defines as special categories of personal data, nor do we make decisions based on ethnicity, race, sex, gender or disability.

title: Privacy and Data Protection
text:
9. Right to Lodge a Complaint
If you consider that your data protection rights have not been properly addressed, you have the right to lodge a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Agency (Agencia Española de Protección de Datos, www.aepd.es).
